Chapter 6: The Quiet Power of Everyday Choices
You know, some of the biggest decisions we ever make don’t really announce themselves. They just slip into our days—almost invisible. Maybe it’s a kind word to a stranger, a promise you keep, or just taking a deep breath instead of snapping when you’re frustrated.
That’s exactly what the father writes about in his letters to Su Yen. He turns his attention to these tiny, often overlooked choices—and how, over time, they quietly shape the whole story of our lives.
He remembers this one morning, years ago. He was running late, stressed out, and when a neighbor asked for help, he snapped. Just a few sharp words—but the regret lingered long after.
It was a tough reminder: who we really are doesn’t show up in those big, dramatic moments... it’s revealed in how we treat others when no one’s paying attention.
Most of us underestimate the ripple effect our small actions can have. A gentle word might ease someone’s day. But a careless remark? That can leave a mark that lasts.
The father also shares a story about a friend of his. This guy had a demanding job—always busy. But every single evening, he still made time to call his aging parents. It wasn’t flashy, and honestly, it would’ve been so easy to skip. But over the years, those calls became a lifeline. They tied the family together, even through illness, loss, and all the changes life throws at you.
What really stands out is this: it’s not about grand, intense gestures. It’s about showing up, day after day. That consistency? That’s what builds real trust and love.
The letters urge Su Yen to notice the choices she makes each day—especially when there’s nobody around keeping score. We live in a world where everyone’s waiting for that “big moment” to shine. But the truth is, real strength comes from quietly doing the right thing, even when it’s inconvenient, or nobody’s there to see it.
There’s something so warm about how he describes daily rituals: brewing tea for someone you love, really listening without distractions, making sure you show up when you said you would.
These aren’t just habits—they’re little ways of saying, “You matter.”
He hopes Su Yen will see the meaning in these small acts, and realize—one choice at a time, that’s how you build a good life.
Of course, nobody gets it right every single day. There’ll be times when impatience wins out, or promises slip by, or the easy way looks too tempting.
But his advice is gentle: don’t be too hard on yourself. What really matters is that you notice, you apologize, and you’re willing to try again.
